blocks.text: DR HUW MAYBERRY (affirmed) (via video link)
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Good morning. Could you state your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So my name is Huw Francis Mayberry.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Could you tell us your current occupation, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I'm employed as a paediatric intensive care registrar at the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, Australia.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: If I could take you back to June 2016, what was your role back then?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then I was a paediatric ST3 trainee, which is the first level on the middle grade rota for paediatric doctors.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. And in June 2016, were you employed at the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: We're going to ask you questions about your involvement with a patient, a baby, by the name of [Baby N], and in particular events on 15 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: We have access to the clinical notes that were prepared on that day and we're able to show them to you on screen, but when doing so you'll see the notes but you won't be able to see the court simultaneously.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay. No problem.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Have you had opportunity to refresh your memory from a statement you made on 10 March 2020?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So I've re-read the statement. Unfortunately, I haven't had access to the notes because of a problem with the EGRESS system, but I've re-read the statement.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. I can show you the note. Your note is actually quite a brief note on the clinical note, so if I could ask my colleague here, Mr Murphy, to put up tile 245 and then show the witness the original document that lies behind it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we go to the bottom of that page, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Mayberry, can you see your own note there at the bottom of the page?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: If you'd like to take a minute or two just to refresh your memory from that note.?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sure.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: (Pause)
Yes, I have read it.
I'm grateful. It's a brief note and your statement goes into quite a bit more detail.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Could you confirm that you were crash bleeped to attend at the neonatal unit just before 15.00 hours on 15 June 2016?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Did you subsequently create this note of these events about 2 hours later?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Upon arrival at the unit and attending upon the baby [Baby N], what were you informed as to the reason why you'd been called?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I was told that he had had a sudden deterioration after 3ml of blood had been aspirated from his nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: What was the nature of the deterioration as communicated to you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So from the notes and the best of my recollection, it appears that he'd had a profound drop in his oxygen levels, which you'd normally expect to be above 92%, down to 44% on my arrival.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Are you able, from this distance of time, to recall who it was who informed you about the 3ml of blood that had been aspirated from his nasogastric tube?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, I can't recall that, sorry.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I understand. So when presented with this baby, who was, as you've described, profoundly desaturating, what intervention did you perform?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I undertook a jaw thrust, which is a procedure to open the airway if it's -- if there's some degree of obstruction for whatever reason, and then proceeded to, in medical slang, bag the patient, which means -- where you ventilate the child's lungs for them and continue to ventilate them until their oxygen saturations were 100%.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you feel comfortable conducting this exercise alone or did you seek some support elsewhere?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Given that there'd been concern about bleeding from the NG tube, and I think earlier on in the day there'd also been concern about bleeding in the upper airway or oropharynx, I bleeped the consultant to attend. I was happy in the procedure of ventilating the patient as I had a lot of experience in that, but I was worried about further complications, hence bleeping Dr Saladi.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Were you cognisant of the fact that the patient was deemed to have a history of haemophilia?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Whilst awaiting the consultant, Dr Saladi, did you explore the airway at all?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So I had one attempt at intubating [Baby N].
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I could see the vocal cords, which is the landmark that you normally look for to put a breathing tube through, but I was unable to get a very clear view because there was quite a -there was a substantial swelling within the airway, so I didn't attempt further and I handed over to Dr Saladi.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I appreciate that several years have passed, but do you have any actual recollection of what you've described as "substantial swelling" within the airway?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the swelling was unlike anything that I'd encountered previously. The epiglottis, which is essentially a flap of tissue that is behind the tongue and that often hangs over the area of the upper airway and the vocal cords, was quite swollen, it looked quite large and sort of reddy-pink in colour. It was more red than the surrounding mucosal tissue. It looked somewhat more rounded than I expected it to and it reminded me of what you sometimes see in textbooks described as epiglottitis, though this -- I had not seen this in my practice before, only in textbooks.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. So just to recover that ground for certainty, your evidence is to the effect this was the first time you'd actually observed this sort of presentation in a neonate or in any patient?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Because my predominant experience in intubating patients up to this point was in neonates, it would be in neonates.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. You described the colour as being more red than the neighbouring tissue; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And you said it was round. Can you expand upon the shape any further?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So with a -- I think I provided a picture potentially, which may have been submitted to you of an epiglottis. It is normally relatively -- it is almost... It is predominantly flat, but it's curved slightly at either end, and normally quite thin. But it appeared to be more, slightly more rounded. I don't know if that related to what I perceived as the inflammation of the epiglottis, the swelling of it, if that had caused it to be more rounded or not.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Mayberry. You have provided some images and we'll look at them in a moment.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sure.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: In your evidence a minute or two ago you said that the swelling provoked you to think of epiglottitis.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Was it your opinion that this was epiglottitis or it reminded you of epiglottitis?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I probably, certainly up to that point as well, don't have the expertise to say whether it was or wasn't. It was reminiscent of what I'd seen described as epiglottitis in textbooks. I had not -- it's not something that I'd seen children of this age have, epiglottitis, it wasn't something I was aware of neonatal -- the neonatal population having as an illness. Most of the experience with epiglottitis relates to an infection called haemophilus influenzae B, which is something which has largely moved out of modern practice thanks to vaccination, but it's described as a sort of much-feared problem in older children when they are being intubated.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. You helpfully provided two images to the investigative team, one, is this right, of a standard, if I may say so, a normal epiglottis, and also, by comparison, an image
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: of an epiglottis where epiglottitis is present, to compare and contrast; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: We're going to put them on screen now. These are the images that you helpfully retrieved from, I think, the internet; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that is correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Could you assist us laymen, please, as to which is which and what it is that we should be looking at here?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay. So I presume you can see the same images that I can see.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: We can.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The image on the left-hand side is rotated through 90 degrees to the left, so it's on its side at the moment. The thing that I have highlighted with a black line is the epiglottis. Between that you can see a sort of dark opening and two bits of tissue either side, which is the tracheal opening and the vocal cords beneath it.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: The image on the right-hand side, I can't remember the exact source, but I did provide it to the police.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: It is an image taken of a child with epiglottitis. So if you look at the two images, the rounded structure appears to be more reddened and swollen on the right-hand side than on the lefthand side.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: The image is now being rotated. Do they now match each other in terms of orientation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. You selected this image, did you, to convey, to communicate, the swelling, the swollen feature; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. The image on the right was the closest to my recollection at that period of time of what the epiglottis looked like.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I'm grateful. So we all understand, you made witness statements in March 2020 and in September 2021; that's correct, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: So you were casting your mind back a few years in any event?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we now --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mr Driver, before we leave the images it might be worth just clarifying in the right-hand image what it is that is surrounded by the epiglottis there.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The large, apparent tube-like structure that the epiglottis is around.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My apologies. The epiglottis is around an inserted endotracheal tube, so a tube going from the outside down into the trachea or the windpipe.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm grateful, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So that explains the image and also gives us some greater understanding of the procedure that you were at least contemplating with [Baby N].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes?
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Mayberry. Can I return to the events of 15 June 2016 now. Did you stay with [Baby N] until Dr Saladi attended?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: From the best of my recollection, yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I wouldn't have left the child without a healthcare professional with him, especially in this case. But to the best of my recollection, I believe I did stay there until Dr Saladi was there. I wasn't there continually as things went on. I did pop back intermittently. The predominant reason for that is I believe I had to cover other parts of the department, so at that point there were other people in place to cover that. But obviously out of concern for [Baby N], when I could, I popped back -- and also to see how other people had got on.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again. Could we have the image of Dr Mayberry back on our screen, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
Thank you.
I'm grateful.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So you had other responsibilities, I'm sure we all understand, but you did return, in your words, intermittently to see how things were progressing with [Baby N]?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Was that the only reason why you returned or was there another reason?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: My main concern was about [Baby N]. I also -- it was predominantly about [Baby N], to be honest. I obviously had a professional curiosity as to how other people had got on in terms of intubating him and if they'd experienced similar difficulty, but my main concern was about [Baby N].
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Did you see any blood at all with this baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Not that I recall, although it obviously is a long time ago now. But I don't recall it, no.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Were you in a position to assess what had or may have caused the swelling at all?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, it's not something I have had much experience of, especially in the neonatal population.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Mayberry.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: My Lord, the only other contribution from Dr Mayberry as recorded on our sequence of events is the prescription of dexamethasone, which I don't think merits taking the doctor to the tile. It was a prescription at 17.35 behind our tile 288 for completeness, but it's not a particularly noteworthy event.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's on the record and so if anyone wants to ask anything about it, they can, or if anyone wants to look at the record they can.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Just finally, Dr Mayberry, do you recall communicating with colleagues at Alder Hey, and in particular the haematology department, and you making an urgent request for factor VIII to be brought to Chester for [Baby N]? Do you recall that?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I believe so, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: I'm grateful. I think there may be some more questions for you, but that's the extent of the questions I have for you this morning, Dr Mayberry.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Mayberry, when you attended [Baby N] after you'd been asked to see him, do you recall whether the blood that had been aspirated was in a pot attached to the tube on free drainage?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I don't recall, I'm sorry.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: All right. As to the blood that had been aspirated, did you consider what possible explanations there might be for that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So I'd been asked previously by the police as to possible reasons, essentially, for why this might be there. The concerns could be related to his factor VIII deficiency, there might be concerns about a gastric erosion or some irritation within the stomach from an indwelling nasogastric tube or concern about necrotising enterocolitis, which is an illness that newborns, particularly premature newborns, can have.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. The link is good given that you're on the other side of the world, but it's occasionally a little bit fuzzy, so I'm just going to go back over what you said so we can follow it clearly here. First of all, did you make reference to gastric irritation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Could you explain what you meant by that as a possible cause for blood?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sure. So sometimes when the lining of the stomach becomes irritated, then the sort of surface tissue can become a bit more friable and sometimes you can have blood coming from that.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: You also made reference, did you, to necrotising enterocolitis?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: We know that's called NEC for short.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: That's something which, with neonates, when there is a potential problem with their stomachs or intestines, that's often a factor that is borne in mind, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Did you also consider whether there was something called haemorrhagic disease of the newborn related to a potential clotting disorder?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That would also factor in related to sort of -whether there was a problem with bleeding related to sort of the factor VIII deficiency. I must say at the time the predominant concern was his airway and so that was where most of the focus was at that point in time.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: We understand that. Just with the question about clotting, you were aware that [Baby N] had been identified as someone with haemophilia, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And that there was what's called a factor VIII deficiency, wasn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: We'll come to your examination in a moment, but can I just confirm with you, Dr Mayberry, that there was a call to the consultant haematologist at Alder Hey, was it that morning, about getting factor VIII?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I believe so. I would have to just look over my statement, but I believe it was that morning.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: All right. Is that because at that point there was no factor VIII on the unit at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't recall, to be honest with you. That could be a potential explanation.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Turning to your examination, Dr Mayberry, in the note that you made at the time, you did identify that there was swelling in the epiglottis, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: As best as you can remember, you didn't identify or see any blood in that area, did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not to my recollection, no.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Is it standard practice that when you are about to perform an intubation, you do examine the area of the trachea and the epiglottis as carefully as you're able to see what's there? That's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. I mean, you'd identify the structures to make sure that you intubated properly, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Was this the first time that you had examined [Baby N] so far as his trachea, his windpipe, his epiglottis was concerned?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: To the best of my recollection, yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: And were you aware that [Dr A] had been involved in an attempted intubation with [Baby N] round about 8 o'clock the same morning --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: -- although we know as a matter of record that was unsuccessful?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: After you'd called Dr Saladi to the unit, did he attempt to intubate [Baby N] as well?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't recall.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: All right. We'll hear more about that from someone else then, Dr Mayberry. Thank you. Those are my questions.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Re-examination by MR DRIVER
Just one area of re-examination. You assisted us with possible, dare I say, hypothetical explanations for the blood. Do you know where the blood originated from?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: As in -- when you say do I know, as in... I was told it came from the nasogastric tube, but that is as much as I have been told.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you. Do you know the explanation for the bleed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Mayberry. They are all the questions I have for you.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Does your Lordship have any questions for the witness?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Mayberry.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Mayberry will be returning to court via the link later this week.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Right. Dr Mayberry, thank you very much for making yourself available this evening to you, because it's quite late at night, I believe, in Australia --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: -- although you were greeted with a "this morning" when we started from Mr Driver because it's morning here of course. That completes your evidence tonight from your point of view, but you will be required, I'm told, on Thursday. I assume a similar arrangement is going -- it'll be the same time on Thursday if you could make yourself available then, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: In the meantime, although I doubt whether there will be anyone out in Australia who may be interested in this, but please don't talk to anyone about anything to do with this case.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Sure.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: That's worldwide, obviously. All right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MAYBERRY

blocks.text: Thank you very much indeed. Thank you for being available tonight.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, the next witness has special measures.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Three or 4 minutes, as quickly as we can anyway. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
(In the absence of the jury)
The photographs that Dr Mayberry provided are exhibits HFM/1 and 2. We'll have to formally exhibit them. Mr Murphy will have them on the additional file for the iPads for [Baby N].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
(In the presence of the jury)
[DR A] (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Could I invite you to state your full name for the recording, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's [Dr A].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: We know from your previous evidence that you worked for a while as a registrar in the paediatric department of the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Today you're going to be asked questions specifically about your involvement in the treatment of a baby by the name of [Baby N] and, in particular, the night shift of the 14th into 15 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I anticipate you've had the opportunity to refresh your memory from witness statements that you have made --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, I have.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- and original clinical notes; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No, not the clinical notes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Not the clinical notes. As per your last visit to the witness box, we have the notes available for you to look at on screen, but before doing so, do you have any direct memory of [Baby N] and your involvement with him?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, I do.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is there anything in particular that made [Baby N] memorable?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: [Baby N] had an unusual clotting disorder or -- not an unusual disorder, it's one of the first times I've seen that clotting disorder in a neonatal unit baby, and I remember as that night went on, he became more unwell and at the end of my night shift, the very beginning of the daytime shift's work, I had been unable to intubate him, which for me is not a frequent occurrence.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you for that summary. Let's focus in on the detail if we may. Mr Murphy, if you could put up tile 80, please. Leave it at that for the moment.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This timeline records that at 01.45 on Wednesday, 15 June, you made notes, or the notes suggest, I should say, that you had cause to attend upon [Baby N].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we click on to the original note, please. Would you like the opportunity to refresh your memory from this note before I ask you any questions?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were you asked to see the patient?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The reason why?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: From the top of my note there, it says:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Asked to see patient regarding mottling and appearance."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. At which point he was 14 days old and had a notional gestational age of 36 weeks, 3 days?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was presumed that he had haemophilia A on the basis of his mother's known medical history. Was he at this point in time self-ventilating in air?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: He was being fed by bottle upon demand?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The rate -- sorry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The next line is:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Increased feeds today to 60ml."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry, we're getting intermittent disruptions to the display. Maybe Mr Astbury is responsible for it. All right. It's back on again now anyway, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Sorry, [Dr A].
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So his feeding regime was progressing?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I believe so, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: His medication was limited, was it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, to vitamins and minerals.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Does the following entry record that which you directly observed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. On examination he was settled, then there was mottling to the torso and limbs.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Pausing there, why would you have recorded the fact that he was "settled"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Because a baby may be in distress, they may be crying, they may be writhing, they may have signs of discomfort following a feed, but [Baby N], at 1.45 in the morning, was settled.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. You observed, as you had been told, that there was mottling to the torso and -- is that all limbs or any particular limbs?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I just said limbs. I don't recall whether that's all or just the upper limbs, lower limbs.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Pausing there, what is the potential significance of mottling in a neonate?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Mottling, it's seen sometimes. It can be to do with illness, it could be a sign of sepsis, meaning that blood flow is being diverted away from the skin.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Usually you would... It's an appearance that makes you want to find the cause for it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that was an appearance, part of his presentation that you noted, and in fact it was the reason why you'd been asked to review him?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But as to the rest of his presentation upon examination, how was he?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: All of the -- the remainder of the examination was normal. His heart rate was normal, his heart sounds were normal, his femoral pulses were normal, his respiratory rate was normal. There was no discrepancy in the sounds of air entering his lungs. His abdomen was soft and there was no enlargement of his liver, either kidneys or spleen, he had active bowel sounds, which suggests good health generally.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. In those circumstances, what significance or explanation would you apply to the mottling?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Well, mottling can sometimes be seen with reflux and he'd been -- I noted there that he'd been fed approximately 45 minutes earlier. But I believe this may have been the first time that I'd met [Baby N] and I wasn't sure what his normal appearance was like.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That is information that you get from the staff looking after him.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Enable the doctor to look further down this note, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did you cause investigations to be undertaken?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. So because of the appearance and because of the concern that had requested me to go there at that time of night, I'd asked for a capillary gas to be performed, a little sample from the foot, with numbers I'm sure you're familiar with.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that a test that generates the results at the cot side?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Within 1 to 2 minutes, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you summarise those results for us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Certainly. His pH is normal at 7.416. His carbon dioxide is normal at 5.43. His bicarbonate is normal or acceptable for a baby of his age at 25.6. His base excess, which is a measure of compensation, is normal. The two numbers on the right-hand side -- his lactate is very slightly elevated and his glucose again is very slightly elevated.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Those elevations of lactate and glucose, what are they indicative of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The lactate can indicate a metabolic disturbance. It is often increased when there's infection. It can be increased if there's poor circulation and it can also be increased if the sample was squeezed as it was taken out. So if it was difficult
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: to get the blood for the sample in the tube, then that extra squeeze can sometimes elevate it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the very act that enables the test can skew that test result?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It can occasionally, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As to glucose?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It is slightly higher than usual. Normal is about 5.4, but again this is 45 minutes after his last food and today was the day that his feeds had been increased to 60ml, so there was probably more glucose content in the feed that he'd had. It's not a worrying number.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Are either of those worrying numbers, lactate or glucose?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The lactate more so.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The degree to which that would cause you worry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I beg your pardon?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: How great a worry is a lactate of 3.2?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So normally I don't expect to see a lactate above 2 unless there's something causing it, but again he examined very well: his observations were normal and the only worrying sign at the time or sign for concern was the mottling. And again, if his skin was mottled, sampling blood from the skin may be the reason that that lactate is slightly elevated.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. And your plan at this stage of the morning?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Observe for now and I will review him within the next 1 to 2 hours.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. And indeed, you did -- and in fairness to you, could [Dr A] be shown the remainder of the note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think some of it is down the bottom of this page.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we keep scrolling down, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So at 03.45, just refresh your memory.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So I've returned to review. Desaturations are noted on the monitor. Five episodes -- I'm sorry, I can't read that word because the annotation is stamped above it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Might it be "whilst on monitor"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Probably. Then on examination, his mottling has resolved. Heart rate remains at 130 beats a minute and is regular.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We'll get to the remainder of your note in a moment.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But focusing on your note that indicates desaturations, 5x episodes, does that inform us that you directly observed desaturations or were they reported to you or don't you know?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I would presume at that time not to have observed five episodes myself. It's most likely that that's been reported to me by the member of staff looking after him for the previous 2 hours.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So if I was to ask you about the time period within which there were five episodes, would you be able to help or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I can't tell you from this notation but I would look at that on the record chart that was at the end of the baby's cot.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Right. Thank you. Could we go to tile 84, please, where I hope there will be a more complete note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There we have the note at the bottom of the first page, which continues through to the next page. Would you like the opportunity to read your own note to refresh your memory?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I've done so, thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So might I ask about his cardiovascular presentation at 03.45?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Certainly. His heart rate, we've already said, is 130 beats per minute and regular. His heart sounds are normal. His abdomen is soft, non-tender. He's not showing any signs of discomfort. He has active movements and -- I have written "no chest distress".
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I would normally meant to have written "no respiratory distress", but it conveys what I've observed. He has vesicular sounds in all zones, so there's no additional unexpected sounds in his breathing, it is a normal chest. And his tone and movement are normal.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I have then said my impression, and I'm wondering whether [Baby N] has an infection.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So at 01.45 you had set yourself the plan to review him within an hour or two. You returned 2 hours later and, in summary, how was he?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: He's changed slightly. So the original concern of mottling has resolved, but I'm now being informed that he's dropped his oxygen saturations within these 2 hours on a number of occasions. That, accompanied by the knowledge that he was mottled earlier, I have then had to consider what that cause is and I'm considering that it might be infection.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So you have just explained to us that the indicators that cause you to consider infection, were there any counterindicators?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No. His tone and movement are normal. He examines normally. But infection can evolve as it establishes itself and I'm believing at this time that I've seen the very beginnings of that process.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we look at your plan, if we could scroll down, Mr Murphy, we'll see what you did to further investigate.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you take us through the plan?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. My first item is screening. This is a septic screen, to take blood for markers of infection and also a blood culture so that if any bacteria are causing this, we may be able to grow them and that would later inform us about changes in antibiotic therapy if required.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: My next plan is IV cefotaxime; it's a first-line antibiotic. He is to remain on the monitor rather than being intermittently monitored. He can continue his oral feeds for the moment. We await the results of the blood tests and, right now, a repeat gas.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do we see immediately below the results of the repeat gas?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you take us through those, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. So this is a reassuring gas. He has a normal pH, his carbon dioxide level is normal, his bicarbonate level is normal. There is a slight increase in his base excess, it was 1 previously, it's now 2.5. His glucose is normal. His lactate has also normalised in the last 2 hours.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you explain to us the significance or otherwise of the increase in the base excess?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Base excess is a marker of how much compensation the body is doing to maintain that normal pH. Acceptable limits for base excess are minus 2 to plus 2, so he's just over, and again, I would normally expect to see a discrepancy in the base excess if there were abnormal pH, PCO2 or bicarbonate. Again, this is a slightly out of range result, but it's not massive, and the rest of the gas is normalised and reassures me, but I'm still concerned as to what's caused the physical symptoms that he's experienced over the last few hours.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And you would look to the blood results to inform you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's what I'm waiting for.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I wonder whether Mr Murphy could put up J19341, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If you could magnify it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We know, [Dr A], that you made a second review of [Baby N] at about 03.45. This document tends to suggest that there was a sample collected from [Baby N] at 03.53 on 15 June under your instruction. Does it flow that this is the bloods that you were awaiting?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Presumed sepsis", that was a sort of presumptive diagnosis on your part?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What do these blood results tell you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: This is a reassuring set of blood test results. CRP is a marker of inflammation, which is a secondary marker of infection, it is low. In fact, it's an unrecordable result, there is no elevation in CRP. The remainder of the tests below that are the full blood count component and his total white cell count is normal, platelets are normal, which are often elevated in an inflammatory process. His haemoglobin is normal. The remaining blood cell counts, the MCV and MCH, are largely to do with red cell performance, they are not really pertinent to what I'm looking at here, but they're a normal component of a full blood count. And the ones down at the bottom, his neutrophil count is normal, which is the white blood cells that usually deal with bacterial infection. His lymphocytes are normal, that's a component that normally deals with a viral infection.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Looking at it globally, do those results tend towards or against the earlier presumed diagnosis?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: At 03.53 when this sample was taken, there was no elevation. Unfortunately, CRP doesn't tend to rise for about 18 hours. There's a lag phase to it of approximately 18 hours. The full blood count component, you're correct to suggest that there is not an inflammatory process going on at this time, but it doesn't always follow that the results are there, and so this might be very early in that process and [Baby N] hasn't yet mounted a response.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I understand. You caused the tests to be taken for a purpose; what purpose did they serve?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: They reassured me that he wasn't mounting a big inflammatory response, there wasn't a big immune response going on, and that reassures me that this is unlikely to be an infective cause, but I still don't know that for sure. The result that will help me there is the blood culture result, which would take 36 to 48 hours to become available.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's move, please, to tile 98. Timed at 05.15. Tile 98 is your third review of [Baby N] this morning. If we can click on the underlying note, please, at 05.15. Would you care to refresh your memory from that note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: (Pause). Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So at this point in time, had you had the opportunity to consider the results that we've just looked at a minute or two ago?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So I've certainly seen them at this time because I've written them in two different places as part of that note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The capillary refill time as of 05.15 was centrally 3 seconds.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. So that's a prolonged capillary refill time.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Normally, I would expect to press on the skin, it will go pale and then refill with blood. Its normal colour appearance should return usually in under 2 seconds.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So this is a little slow, sluggish?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: A little.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What is that indicative of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It suggests that blood flow to the skin is being diverted elsewhere for some other purpose. Usually, peripheral capillary refill time prolongs before central capillary refill time. So the fact that I've got prolonged cap refill centrally suggests to me that this is slightly more serious and needs taking account of.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is it a sign of infection, dehydration or what?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's a non-specific sign. It can represent both of those things. It just suggests that the volume of blood is not being delivered to the skin in the way that is normal.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So the list of digits on the left, are they some of the data that you'd extracted from the results that we considered previously?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's what I considered pertinent. I've obviously looked at the whole record, but I've written in the pertinent results here.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Where it says HB, I think it's 139. Let's go to the right of the page. Could you decode that note for us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's turgor and I have put an N with a circle. This is skin turgor. It's the sign where you gently pinch the skin and lift it. And as you let go, you watch for how that skin behaves. If you're dehydrated and underfilled, you get some tenting of that skin and it takes a long time to settle back down to the normal skin surface appearance.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So is this a measure of the elasticity of the skin?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's a measure more of volume of fluid that's there. If you are underfilled, if there is not enough blood volume, dehydration essentially, then that skin turgor is prolonged, and in [Baby N] I've said that his skin turgor is normal.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And the note beneath that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: "Femorals ++."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I've undone his nappy and felt both the pulses in his femorals. I recorded them as "++" which just means that they're normal. There's nothing abnormal about them. It's not that they're unusual in any way.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. And the plan as of 05.15?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Based on that capillary refill time being slightly prolonged and he now has mottling, I've said a bolus of 10ml per
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: kilogram of body weight with normal sodium chloride, I'm going to stop his oral feeds and give him his volume of fluid per day as IV glucose, and I'm presuming at the time I looked at these results the CRP wasn't available, but we saw it all in one document on the previous screen and then obviously the CRP has become available and I've written the result at the end of my note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is the bolus of saline intended to improve his circulation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did you ever have the opportunity to see whether it had achieved that objective?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I recall seeing him later on into that night.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's go to tile 143, please, Mr Murphy. It takes us to a note written at 08.00 hours. If you could refresh your memory from it first, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: (Pause)

Firstly, as to the timing of the review of [Baby N], if I could tell you, [Dr A], it's not controversial, at tile 142 of our chronology here there is swipe data of you entering the maternity neonatal entrance doors at 07.16 hours.
DR A: I may have been asked to see other children on the unit.
I may have looked at [Baby N] first, I don't recall.
Obviously, I'd been busy that night, back and to. If I've entered the unit at 7.16, it may be for some other reason than this patient.
Understood. But in any event, the timing of the writing of the note --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Is at 8 am, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The reason why you reviewed [Baby N] prior to the note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: My note says that I've been:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Asked to review due to a profound desaturation down to 48% and a drop in heart rate."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You use the adjective "profound". How significant a desaturation is that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's a concerning desaturation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: How significant is a drop of heart rate to about 80 beats per minute?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: A brief desaturation or a desaturation that doesn't go very low in percentage terms usually doesn't affect heart rate. The fact that the oxygen supply to the child's tissues is down to 48% means that there's been enough to affect heart rate and reduce it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We know from your notes and from your evidence that you, amongst other times, reviewed [Baby N] at 03.45 --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- at which point your note alludes to five episodes of desaturations at that point in time. In terms of degree, how do the two compare, 03.45 to this as noted at 08.00 hours?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I haven't recorded those in my note and it would be likely that I would have used the child's record chart at the end of the cot to look at those.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think you have a paper version. Not that file, [Dr A]. The one nearest me, I think that's the one, behind divider 18.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Both 16 and 18 are empty.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: (Pause)
Can I pass up, through Mr Worthington, a bundle of documents?
(Handed)
Apologies for that, [Dr A].
DR A: Thank you.
There are half a dozen or so documents there.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Observation chart...
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: (Pause).
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do those documents assist at all?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: They show his progress over the night and certainly starting at 9 pm... Sorry, starting at 1 am, they show me that his oxygen levels at 1 am were recorded as normal and this looks as though it's a scheduled check, as do the results at 5 am.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm struggling to make out the time of the next entry; I assume that's 7 am. His oxygen saturations have been recorded at 100% for those times.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So oxygen at 100% at 7 am, if your reading of the handwriting is correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But by the time you examined him at some point prior to 8 in the morning --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- his sats had dropped to 48%?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. I'm just looking at the 7 am entry again.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It would appear that he is on -- it looks as though he is receiving 25% oxygen at that time and that's maintaining his oxygen saturations at 100%. I suspect that this follows the five episodes of desaturation that were recorded earlier in the night.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Are you aware the method through which that 25% oxygen was being supplied to [Baby N]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It will have been either through nasal cannulae or a mask.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Because we know that he wasn't intubated and therefore wasn't being ventilated?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: At the start of the night he was self-ventilating in air and I would have been called if he'd needed any other way of administering the oxygen.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that non-invasive form of assistance was sufficient to have him 100% saturated?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It would appear so. At 9 am the record is that he is 100% in air. So clearly, this changes sometimes more frequently than the lines on the chart allow the recording.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Understood. So let's go back to your review of [Baby N] as written up at 08.00 hours. So he desaturated to 48%, the heart rate correspondingly low?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And so what remedial action did you take?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The next line says that he was being bagged using a Neopuff circuit. This is the equipment at the cot side that has a mask to be placed over the infant's mouth and nose.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: And a bag method of squeezing a certain percentage of oxygen into the infant to restore their oxygen saturations.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And his skin at this point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It says, "Mottled appearance and reduced tone". So since my last review of [Baby N], his mottling, I think at 5 am, I'd said, had returned, but at the time he had normal tone and now he's not as responsive as he was, he doesn't handle in the same way.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So your use of "reduced" in this note is comparative --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- as compared to your --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: To my previous examination.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Having considered all these features, what did you determine was necessary in the circumstances?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: [Baby N] needed more assistance than could be provided in one of the lower numbered nurseries. So he's moved through to nursery 1, which allowed me to have more equipment available and more opportunities for interventions to be performed.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You've had the benefit of reminding yourself of this note at this point, but might I invite you to step back from the note for a moment. Do you remember this event, the event that caused you to have [Baby N] moved from one of the lower nurseries to nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I don't remember the move. I remember entering nursery 1 because I think I may have helped push the cot or the bassinet that the baby was in. My recollection is more of what happened in the next hour or so.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which we'll come to shortly. But at this point in the sequence were you acting alone or with others and, if so, can
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: you remember who else was looking after [Baby N] with you at that point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: At this time, so between me starting to see [Baby N] and moving through to nursery 1, I... This time of sort of 7 to 8 am is when the nursing shift changes, so there will have been more people on the unit having handover and taking over care of different babies.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Does it flow from that that you can't remember who was involved or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I don't recall who was involved, but I obviously know because I can see on the remainder of the observation chart what's initialled.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Thank you. Let's go down the note, please. So he was being bagged or Neopuffed at this point. Was that sufficient, at least in the short term, to maintain his stability?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I've said that as we move, he's continued to maintain saturations with facial oxygen. Now, I presume that he doesn't require bagging at this point because he's been bagged up using the Neopuff circuit and I have just said facial oxygen, so I presume this is oxygen that's the cylinder on the cot or incubator and that's being delivered to him via a face mask.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were you content for that to continue or did you wish to alter things at this point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No, [Baby N] is now concerning me, more so than earlier in the night. And because of his earlier run of five desaturations and now this profound desaturation with reduction in heart rate, I'm not prepared to leave [Baby N] to maintain his own airway and oxygenation. And the next section of the note shows that we've given drugs in preparation for intubation and then that would lead to mechanical ventilation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Pausing there, when we began your evidence, you said that you recalled [Baby N] and recalled these events in part because there was a difficult intubation --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- which stands out in your memory because you were an experienced intubator at the time and were unaccustomed to having difficulties?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: How clear a recollection do you have of the intubation attempts?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I remember the position of the incubator within nursery 1. I remember standing to the side of the incubator in preparation for doing the intubation and the appearance of the oropharynx of [Baby N] as I was trying to intubate him.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So you have a memory of that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I do.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Looking at the note, it says:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Attempted intubation x3."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It tells us of the size of the tube and the technique, the neck roll. Could you explain what that is for us before we go any further?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. The natural position of a baby's head when laid on their back makes it difficult to intubate without supporting their neck and using -- it's often a nappy that's rolled, a disposable nappy, because they're quite small. It can be anything, but a roll that just sits in the nape of the neck before the protuberance at the back of the head, and that prevents the baby's neck from flattening, which then reduces the height of the trachea, the air inlet. So by putting the roll there, I can guarantee that I'm not going to be prevented from seeing where the tube needs to go because the baby's position is wrong.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you for that explanation. What did you see?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So I... I was stood slightly to the left of [Baby N] but certainly behind him. He at that time had been rotated within the incubator and there is a little shelf that pulls out so that his feet remain in the incubator but his head, neck and part of his chest protrudes from it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It means that the laryngoscope, which I held in my left hand, wouldn't then knock on the lid of the incubator and it means that I can manipulate the laryngoscope and insert the tube. It also means that he's outside of the incubator ready for all of the things that need to happen to secure that tube in place once it's been positioned.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you remind us what a laryngoscope is, please, and what is its function?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The laryngoscope is a device that provides light and a mechanical way of lifting the baby's tongue up so that you can see past that bit of their mouth and throat to where the entry to the trachea is. Typically, it contains two small batteries and it's very similar to the device that you look in ears and eyes, it's just that it has a different attachment to it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So was it through the laryngoscope that you viewed [Baby N]'s oropharynx?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, because on his back, laying down, his tongue would droop with gravity and without him sort of being able to hold it in the correct position -- so for all intubations a laryngoscope is used of to provide light and mechanical support to the tongue to lift it up so you can see where the tube is required to go.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And what did you see down the laryngoscope on this occasion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I saw blood at the back of the throat. I saw blood that prevented me from seeing where the entry to his airway was.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did that, in effect, impede your attempted intubation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I couldn't see where I was aiming to position the tube.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In addition to blood, did anything else catch your attention?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I recall that the back of [Baby N]'s throat did not look — it looked unusual. There was a degree of swelling, I recall. I can't picture that -- that would have been at the sort of upper aspect of my view and I was concentrating on the lower aspect where the blood was and where I was aiming to position the tube.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Taking them in turn, separately, which did you notice first, the blood or the swelling? Are you able to say?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I think it will been the blood because that's such an unusual thing to see at the time of intubating.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were you able to discern where the blood was coming from?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No, I wasn't.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Moving to the swelling, were you able to discern what caused the swelling?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No. I noted that the swelling was there and the anatomy of babies has a degree of variation anyway and having never had the
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: opportunity to look at or having to perform this procedure on [Baby N] before, I wasn't sure whether this was long-standing or whether this was new.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It must have been unusual for me to have remembered it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This was the first time that you'd looked at [Baby N] through a laryngoscope?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It was, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did you succeed in intubating [Baby N]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No, I didn't.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did you abandon attempts?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I did.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Why?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I abandoned because I've had three attempts at that time and I was concerned because of his haemophilia that if I persisted, the metal blade on the laryngoscope, it's not sharp, it has smoothed edges, but the metal blade, as it's used to lift the tongue up out of the way, a little bit like a spatula, to lift the tongue up, I didn't want to cause any mechanical damage with the laryngoscope. And at this time, 8 to 9 am, there will have been more staff arriving and I was able -- I think we'll find a little bit lower down, I've given my reasoning for abandoning.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I have said that I was unable to visualise the tracheal inlet and that suction did not clear the view.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's common for there to be mucous secretions, maybe some milk, clear fluids usually, the sort of physiological fluids that are removed by suction.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Normally, that degree of suction allows you to have a clear view without any mucous reflecting light or causing bubbles. But unfortunately the suction that was being done did not clear my view of the blood enough to allow me to intubate. So I've abandoned due to the blood present in the oropharynx and I have stopped because I don't want to carry on failing to intubate and cause more -- well, any mechanical trauma.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Would you have taken that course absent haemophilia? So if [Baby N] was not suspected to be a haemophiliac, would you have continued to attempt to intubate even with the presence of blood or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The haemophilia was certainly a big element in this.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I would usually not persist after three attempts unless it was a life-and-death situation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's continue considering your note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The next line says that we've commenced [Baby N] on BiPAP, so non-invasive ventilation. The machine was set with a back-up rate of 30 breaths per minute.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. And is that a measure of his blood pressure and his refill time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right. So his blood pressure is acceptable at 81/55 and his capillary refill time has remained at 3 to 4 seconds.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And the standard return is at 2 seconds; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right, that's normal.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the plan of action?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Because of the prolonged capillary refill time, and also because that blood pressure is okay, but I'm presuming because of the capillary refill time that his circulating volume is not as good as I would like it to be, he's having another bolus of 10ml per kilogram of sodium chloride to help boost that circulating volume of his blood.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Was this the extent of your involvement with [Baby N] on this shift?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I will have -- I've requested a chest X-ray, and then I will have handed over to the oncoming day shift.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't recall whether that was back on the children's ward where handover normally takes place or whether somebody came through to the neonatal unit because they will have heard that I was busy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Even though your shift ended, were you sufficiently concerned about [Baby N] to make enquiries as to his well-being after your shift whilst you were off duty?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, I was.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did they include communicating with your colleagues in the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did you make any enquiries of anybody else, any other colleagues outwith the Countess, do you recall?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I don't think so.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER
