blocks.text: When you saw blood, was that in the oropharynx?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, it was.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was it from the oropharynx?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I don't know where the source of the bleeding was, I'm afraid.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: When did you first visualise blood?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I believe it was on my first attempt when I had the laryngoscope blade in my left hand lifting the tongue up out of the way. I believe I saw blood there the first time but I... I don't have... I can't remember the three individual attempts at intubation. I can remember collectively starting and then I remember the discussion at the end about moving on to BiPAP.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. I have no further re-examination.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Does your Lordship have any questions for [Dr A]?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't, thank you very much. Thank you, [Dr A], for coming back and giving evidence again.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes or no?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: You will be coming back again, but that's it, so what I have said to you before still applies: please don't talk to anyone about anything to do with this case. Please remain seated where you are.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, members of the jury. Could you be ready, please, to continue -- I don't know whether it would cause inconvenience if we started at just before 2 o'clock for anyone.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Not from the prosecution's perspective.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't mind, my Lord. It's kind of you to ask.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We'll fit in with whatever time suits the court.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We'll say 1.55. You may think it's pernickety, 5 minutes, but they all add up.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: 1.55, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The short adjournment)
(In the presence of the jury)
May I call Dr John Gibbs, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR JOHN GIBBS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Good afternoon, Dr Gibbs. Could you state your full name again for the record?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm John Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You've been invited this afternoon to give evidence in relation to your involvement with the baby [Baby N]. Were you the on-call consultant in the evening and overnight into 15 June 2016?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I was.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And did you first become involved with [Baby N] shortly before 18.00 hours on 15 June 2016?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did you effectively receive a handover of responsibility from your consultant colleague, Dr Saladi, at about that time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In so doing, were you appraised by Dr Saladi of the events and presentation of [Baby N] in the preceding hours?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I was.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did you appraise yourself of his clinical history?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: He was born on 2 June 2016, so by the time we reach the events of 15 June 2016, he'd been within the unit for the best part of 2 weeks; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And in summary, how would you describe his course over that period?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, up until the 15 June, it had been progressing very well. He had some initial respiratory difficulties in the first day of life, not unexpected for his gestation, and then he had been nicely settled and established on feeds and, I understood, was ready to go home at the time he started to deteriorate on the 15th.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Could I invite Mr Murphy, please, to take us to tile 247, which is a set of clinical notes made by Dr Saladi, who briefed you. If we could go to those.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see what it is that Dr Saladi -- if we could scroll down, please -- recorded at 16.30. So what was the picture as portrayed to you upon you assuming responsibility this early evening?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, [Baby N] was in an unusual situation in that he'd been deteriorating since the night-time before the day of the 15th, so in the early hours of the 15th he started to deteriorate in various ways, which presumably you've heard from [Dr A] this morning, so I won't say anymore about that. But I knew he'd been deteriorating during the night.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: An attempt -- I was aware an attempt had been made to place an endotracheal tube into him at about 8 o'clock in the morning and it wasn't possible to do that, but he'd been put on BiPAP respiratory support and he'd been stable on that for some hours until, as Dr Saladi reports here, at 2.50 pm or 14.50, he was on BiPAP support when he started to desaturate repeatedly and it was felt at that time he needed ventilation support. That's full ventilation support.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So various attempts were made by several people to place an endotracheal tube, but none of those attempts were successful.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Because of the lack of success, did you discover that your colleagues had communicated with both the ear, nose and throat team and also anaesthetists from Alder Hey Hospital?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I understood a team was on its way or was setting off from Alder Hey Hospital in the early evening to come and support us in Chester with managing [Baby N]'s airway.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. In the meantime, did you learn that your colleague Dr Brearey had inserted a laryngeal mask airway into [Baby N]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, and that's what I saw was inserted at the time I first saw [Baby N] that evening.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The jury have heard lots of descriptions of endotracheal tubes and their connection to mechanical ventilation, but I'm not sure we've had an explanation about the laryngeal mask route. Can you help us understand that better?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Right. If I could briefly recap on the endotracheal tube. Just to remind the jury, that's a thin tube that goes through the vocal cords, through the larynx and rests inside the windpipe, and then passes out through the mouth and is connected to ventilator tubing through which a child can be ventilated.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: A laryngeal mask air, which is a long tube, fatter than an endotracheal tube, because it doesn't need to fit inside the airway, it just fits in the back of the throat. It goes over the tongue, down the first part of the back of the throat. At the end of the laryngeal mask airway is an oval-shaped soft flexible mask which -- the usual mask you might have seen rests over the nose and mouth when you're putting a mask over a patient, this is a much smaller version that fits inside the back of the throat, attached to a fat tube, and that little oval mask sits just above the larynx, just above the windpipe at the back of the throat. It's not inserted through the vocal cords into the windpipe, it sits above it.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But it is possible to ventilate through a laryngeal mask airway because the top end of the airway, the rather thick tube, is connected again to ventilator tubing connected to a ventilator, through which ventilation can be given.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is essentially the difference between the two a question of security?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, and where they rest inside the airway. The endotracheal tube, fitting right down inside the airway, so it's more secure and less liable to be dislodged.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The laryngeal mask airway sits just above the voice box, down inside the back of the throat, just above the voice box, and can be dislodged a little more easily.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could I also add, though, that when ventilating a patient, if you need anything higher than low pressures it's much more effective to ventilate down through an endotracheal tube that's inside the windpipe because all the oxygen and air is being directed down the tube into the airway. With a laryngeal mask airway it sits above the voice box so a fair
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: amount of the oxygen and gas air is being directed down into the windpipe, but not all of it, like an endotracheal tube, and it's sometimes difficult to generate high pressures if you need a lot of pressure to inflate the lungs because the mask is sitting just above the windpipe, the tube isn't down inside the windpipe.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So was [Baby N] being ventilated via a laryngeal mask airway at the point that you first saw him on this day?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, at around 6 o'clock in the evening when I first saw him he was being ventilated satisfactorily through the laryngeal mask airway.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we could go to your corresponding note, please, tile 291. Click on to the original note, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We see your handwriting at the top of the page --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- timed at 17.50. Could you tell us what this informs us of, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: One of the first actions I took when I'd been told about -- I had the handover about [Baby N] was to contact our local ear, nose and throat registrar as an initial point of contact with our local ear, nose and throat team. I knew a team, including a consultant ear, nose and throat specialist, was on its way from Alder Hey Hospital in Liverpool but my worry was, just in case [Baby N]'s airway needed help before that team arrived, I wanted our local ENT specialists to know about his problems in case their help was needed.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So I phoned the -- well, I bleeped and then phoned the registrar in ear, nose and throat surgery at the Countess of Chester Hospital -- I'll call him Dr Umesh because that's what he called himself, he had a much longer surname that is written in the surname that I can't read properly, but...
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So Dr Umesh. I informed him about [Baby N] and his difficult airway, requiring LMA, laryngeal mask airway, and the type of laryngeal mask airway he had was called an I-Gel airway, that's why I have put that in brackets, and he is needing that for ventilation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then I have just recorded that:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "He [meaning Dr Umesh] or a colleague will come to assess, but knows that the Alder Hey ENT team are also involved."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: My concern about [Baby N] particularly is that I had been told, and I could see in the notes, that several of the people, which included two anaesthetists from the Countess of Chester Hospital, two registrars and two of my consultant colleagues, several of them had written that they'd noticed a swollen epiglottis, that's the flap of tissue just above the windpipe, and one registrar had written that there was swelling just below the epiglottis. So it is a worry knowing that someone has an airway with a swelling above it because that might block off the airway, which is why I wanted our local ENT colleagues to be aware of the problem in case we needed their help urgently before the ENT team and their specialists had arrived from Alder Hey.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If I can ask you to consider the corresponding note from the anaesthetist you referred to as Dr Umesh -- the ENT registrar, forgive me, not the anaesthetist. I think it's behind tile 304, Mr Murphy, but certainly J19179.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There we have an untimed but dated note to the effect that you, Dr Gibbs, consultant in neonatology, informed, et cetera.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So does that just -- is that his side of that conversation --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- that you described to us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is there anything additional in this note that adds to that which you've already explained to us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No. As you point out, it's not timed and this must be some time after about 8.15 or later because he does refer to the collapse at around 7 o'clock in that. Yes, in this second paragraph after the discussed with Mr Temple, who's a consultant ENT surgeon at the Countess of Chester hospital, he is referring to the collapse that subsequently [Baby N] suffered from. So he wrote this some time after 8.15 or later.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: He also mentioned, which I haven't mentioned but I'm sure the jury is already aware of from [Baby N]'s history, and I was informed of this to make clear, I realised this could be a problem, that [Baby N] suffers or was known to suffer from haemophilia.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you. So just going back then to your note that we've just looked at behind our tile T291, at that point in time what was the plan of action for the management of [Baby N]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The plan of action was to continue the ventilations through the laryngeal mask airway as long as that continued satisfactorily, to await the team, the specialist team arriving from Alder Hey, and the plan is they would then try -- or one of that team would try to intubate [Baby N]. They may -- if they weren't successful in intubating and [Baby N]'s airway seemed to be blocked off, they would perform a tracheostomy. That's a surgical hole created in the front of the windpipe in the neck to assist with breathing.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's move to tile 292, which records the arrival of the Alder Hey team. Click behind there, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This is a note of yours, the note written at 22.05?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Does it set out your involvement and the sequence of events from about 18.00 hours?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could you assist us understand this? What's the recorded time for the arrival of the Alder Hey team?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think it was 17.20. I can't see it in my note here, but it was 17.20. Now, before my note we're looking at now, one of our registrars, [Dr D], had written a detailed account of what had happened in the previous 2 hours and it's in her account she records the ENT as arriving at about 17.20 -- well, sorry, the Alder Hey team, which included a ENT consultant and two other specialists.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: When you say 17.20 --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- I think you might mean 19.20.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry, yes, 7.20 pm.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. The team consisted of Dr Potter?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is he or she an experienced consultant anaesthetist?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, he's a very experienced consultant anaesthetist at Alder Hey and also an intensive care consultant.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Dr Lakin?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Who is another intensive care consultant from Alder Hey Hospital in Liverpool.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And a Ms Day?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. She's a consultant ENT surgeon from Alder Hey Hospital.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. So you told us of what might happen with regards to this team and [Baby N]. Was that intended to take place in Chester or post-transfer to Alder Hey?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was intended to take place in Chester and once the team arrived at 19.20, the plan was to take [Baby N] through to the obstetric operating theatre, that's just down the corridor, a short distance from the neonatal unit in Chester. It is used for caesarean section operations on the labour ward, but it's also used for emergency paediatric surgery.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It wasn't planned definitely to perform any surgery on [Baby N]. The plan was to take him to the obstetric operating theatre where the anaesthetists and intensive care consultants could anaesthetise him so he will be quiet and totally compliant. They would then try to intubate him. If they couldn't intubate him and his airway blocked off, then Ms Day, the consultant ENT surgeon, would perform emergency surgery to create a hole in the front of his neck into his windpipe through which a breathing tube could be inserted; that's a tracheostomy. But that's only if the airway blocked off, which, when you have a difficult airway and you know that several colleagues have noticed the top of the airway is swollen, is a possibility and the airway may block off completely when you try to intubate.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that was the plan. But did events intervene at about 19.40?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. As part of that plan, I forgot to mention one other technique they were going to use to try and facilitate intubation was called a flexible bronchoscopy. That's using a flexible camera with a light that you place into the airway so you can see the airway and then you pass an endotracheal tube over that flexible bronchoscope.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that was -- I was taken up with trying to arrange with other colleagues at the Countess of Chester Hospital to obtain a flexible bronchoscope with the light source that they needed in
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: the operating theatre and that had just arrived some time around 19.30/19.40, and we were planning to take [Baby N] through to the operating theatre when he suddenly deteriorated.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Were you with [Baby N] when he suffered this sudden deterioration?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was in or next to nursery room 1 discussing with various colleagues the equipment they needed to take to the operating theatre when, I can't remember exactly who, but someone called out for help with [Baby N] within nursery room 1. I went over to him at that stage.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you for that. Could you illustrate for us the nature and the extent of this sudden deterioration?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby N] had dropped his oxygen saturation levels down to about 80% and his heart rate had dropped to around 60, and then whilst I was trying to assess him with other colleagues from the Alder Hey team who'd arrived and who came with me to assess [Baby N], his oxygen saturations dropped further to about 40%. And it was clear he was not being ventilated properly at that time with his laryngeal mask airway still in site.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the laryngeal mask airway was still, as you've phrased it, in site?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In situ I should have said, really.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But it wasn't achieving the desired objective?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No. [Baby N] wasn't being oxygenated and his heart rate was slowing down because of that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: How would you describe the degree or seriousness of that desaturation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was a serious, worrying desaturation, but the initial response is to provide breathing support for [Baby N] and it was a colleague, Dr Lakin, one of the intensive care specialists who'd come from Alder Hey, who took over managing [Baby N]'s airway. He initially tried to ventilate him with a bag and mask through his laryngeal mask but couldn't get any chest movement so his ventilation wasn't working at all. So he removed the laryngeal mask airway and applied a face mask straight to [Baby N]'s mouth and nose and started to bag him with oxygen through that face mask.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Going back in time a minute or two, you told us that you were in discussions with colleagues about [Baby N] when your attention was drawn to him and his deterioration.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you recall which colleagues you were in discussion with?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Um... As far as I remember, it was the three consultants from Alder Hey Hospital plus operating department professionals. They are technical staff who help with operating department equipment, particularly anaesthetic equipment, and they had arranged for the flexible bronchoscope and light source to be brought to the neonatal unit. So I was talking to them about the bronchoscopy that needed to be undertaken in [Baby N].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Can you recall whether or not [Dr D] was part of that discussion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't remember where [Dr D] was at that time. She was involved in the resuscitation of [Baby N] but just at the time [Baby N] collapsed I can't remember where she was, no.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's return then to the events. You told us that Dr Lakin was able to provide ventilation through a bag and mask device; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. But [Baby N] didn't respond well. I can't remember his saturations but his heart rate remained low, which is a worry when the heart rate has not improved.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Therefore chest compressions were started and I helped to give those chest compressions.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that was you together with Dr Lakin?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Was that intervention successful?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, in that [Baby N]'s heart rate still did not improve.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: At this stage we started to give him some intravenous adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Can you recall how many doses of adrenaline were given?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In all, six doses were given during the roughly half hour resuscitation. But a key intervention after the second or third dose of adrenaline was that Dr Potter, the consultant anaesthetist and intensivist from Alder Hey, attempted to intubate [Baby N] with an endotracheal tube and successfully managed to do so the first time. And that significantly improved ventilation with good chest movements after the endotracheal tube had been passed.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So a successful intubation, which enabled [Baby N] to be connected to a ventilating machine?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Well, he could have been -- sorry, he could have been connected to a ventilation machine but Dr Potter continued to ventilate by hand.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: My mistake. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But he was provided with ventilation through the endotracheal tube.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And you told us --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm sorry, could I just interrupt you?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Would you mind just pushing the microphone away a little bit, please? Thank you. We are getting a slight -- and it's probably because of the sensitivity of the microphone. We'll see if that's any better. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr Driver.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Not at all, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So six doses of adrenaline, you said, over approximately 30 minutes. I think the records suggest it was between 19.47 and 20.09, which is about 30 minutes, but just so as we are certain as to the time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So this resuscitation, how significant a response was this and how significant a deterioration had [Baby N] suffered?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, it was a very serious, life-threatening deterioration, and the worry was that at first [Baby N] was not responding to the resuscitation efforts by Dr Lakin supporting his ventilation, me supporting his breathing by -- his heart by pressing on his chest, and still his heart rate wasn't improving. So he took time to improve. But he did start to steadily improve after he'd been intubated. It wasn't a complete improvement because he still needed several doses of -- further doses of adrenaline, even after he'd been intubated by Dr Potter.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. By 20.10 hours had you, the team, managed to raise his heart rate to a point where it was regularly above 100 beats per minute?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it was above 100 beats per minute and he no longer needed chest compression to support his circulation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Was he then attached to a ventilating machine?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, I think Dr Potter -- I believe he's going to give evidence later so he can confirm this, I think he carried on hand ventilation after that. But he was being ventilated, provided with artificial ventilation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Anaesthetists are very used to performing hand ventilation of patients, they sometimes do it throughout a patient's operation, for example. They don't always use a ventilation machine, so I think it was Dr Potter doing the ventilating but [Baby N] needed to be ventilated.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. How was he following the resuscitation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, he was much improved as far as his various parameters, observation parameters were concerned. His oxygen levels, his heart rate, had returned to normal.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And he was no longer needing chest compression support.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But he still needed to be artificially ventilated so he still needed intensive care support and, in fact, I think Dr Lakin probably did this more because he'd anticipated, after a half hour resuscitation, that [Baby N] would need continuous support. He started an adrenaline infusion. So that's not adrenaline doses, the large doses we give during resuscitation, that's a very small continuous dose of adrenaline to support the heart and blood pressure. So he needed an adrenaline infusion after that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Was it the plan to summons a paediatric transport team?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. [Baby N] needed then to go to an intensive care unit to be supported, but the transport team to take him to intensive care had already been requested around about the time that the specialist team arrived from Alder Hey. The transport team were getting together to come to collect [Baby N], so in fact the team arrived shortly after the resuscitation had finished. They weren't that fast at getting from Liverpool, they were already on their way. It was sort of part of the plan with the specialist team that had come over from Alder Hey that [Baby N] would be taken off to an intensive care unit elsewhere.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think the records show that they arrived at about 20.40 hours, which fits in with your chronology.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Half an hour/25 minutes after resuscitation had finished, but they were on their way probably during the resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Indeed. We know that [Baby N] was moved from Chester to Alder Hey --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- that night.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So taking a step back, and considering all that you learned and witnessed, what were your conclusions as to the events of 15 June?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was unsure what had caused [Baby N]'s deterioration.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I knew he'd been deteriorating during the night, during the early hours of the morning, and I also knew his chest X-ray taken at around 9 o'clock in the morning had shown some shadowing on the right of his chest that could be infection. Knowing he had haemophilia it perhaps could have been a bleed into his lung because, as you probably would have heard from [Dr A], I was aware that when various colleagues had tried to intubate [Baby N], they had noticed blood in and around his airway.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So possibly it might have been a bleed into his lungs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What I couldn't understand is why two consultant paediatric colleagues, two registrar paediatricians and two consultant anaesthetist paediatricians had not been able to intubate him and three of those at least had recorded in the notes there was swelling around the airway, and yet Dr Potter managed to intubate first time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But a couple of things had happened in between those different attempts. After the unsuccessful attempts during the afternoon, [Baby N] had been given a dose of intravenous high dose steroid called dexamethasone.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That was at the request of the Countess of Chester anaesthetists who had tried to intubate him.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Dexamethasone is very potent at reducing swelling. It's a medication that's given if there's brain swelling after a head injury to reduce the pressure inside the skull. Now, for [Baby N], it was given to try and reduce the swelling around his airway.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Also, shortly after Dr Potter had intubated [Baby N] successfully, he'd been given at least two, I think, looking at the records, maybe three doses of intravenous adrenaline as part of his resuscitation. And adrenaline is a powerful drug at
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: stimulating the heart, which is why we use it in resuscitation. It also reduces swelling around the airway, which is why people, for example, who have severe allergic reactions and if they come into contact with the thing that causes their allergy, like a peanut if they have a peanut allergy, their airway and voice box can swell up and they can stop breathing and it can be lethal and they carry an adrenaline pen, which is -- they should inject themselves or stander-by (sic) should inject them with.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And because [Baby N] had had two doses at least of adrenaline -this was a few hours after the potent intravenous steroid -perhaps the reason all the colleagues had failed to intubate him early, but the reason Dr Potter managed to intubate him straightaway -- but Dr Potter is going to come to talk to the court about this -- perhaps it was because these medications had reduced whatever swelling was there.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Why [Baby N] had that swelling in his airway, which had been documented by several colleagues, I really don't know.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You mentioned X-rays, so for the sake of completeness could we go to tile 176, please, Mr Murphy, which includes Dr Wright's consideration of a radiograph taken at 09.08. I think that's the one you referred to a few moments ago.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Approximately 9.10, you told us. If we can click behind, please. Was this something that you appraised yourself of during your care of [Baby N]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Not this report because I think -- if we can see a little higher up on the report, please -- it says underneath -- on the right-hand side -- hospital number, account number, responsible doctor. And underneath that, "Date typed", and it was typed on the 16th.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So it's been reported and typed the day after the events we're talking about. So I did see the X-ray, and this is a report of the X-ray, so indirectly I knew -- didn't know this report, I saw the X-ray this report is about.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What did you glean from the X-ray itself when you considered it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There was some shadowing on the right-hand side. As I mentioned, that could have been infection and [Baby N] was being covered for infection, as we often do with an ill neonate, cover for infection and check for infection before doing anything else
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: because the infection takes several days to show whether they're positive or not.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But because blood had been seen in his airway because he had haemophilia, the shadowing on his X-ray on the right-hand side might also have been a bleed into his lung.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Dr Wright here in her report is saying that she thinks a pulmonary haemorrhage is less likely but I still, on the night of 15 June, thought it possible there was a haemorrhage particularly because colleagues had seen blood in the airway.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. There was another X-ray taken at 21.07, which we have behind tile 421. So about 12 hours later, almost exactly 12 hours later. Did you consider this X-ray, the radiograph on the time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. The report is typed up again the day after, but this is the X-ray that was taken after resuscitation had been completed, after Dr Potter had successfully intubated [Baby N], and also Dr Potter inserted an intravenous line -- I'm trying to get control... This is the tube (indicating). This is the endotracheal tube running down [Baby N]'s airway (indicating). This white line down the right side of his neck (indicating) is an intravenous line inserted into a vein into [Baby N]'s neck.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And we can see the heart in the middle and the lungs either side, but this whiteness, hazy whiteness (indicating) throughout the lungs is more shadowing than you normally see in the lungs. This could be infection that's got worse from the X-ray in the morning.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: This may be bleeds in the lungs, but if it is, it's very extensive bleeds on both sides. Or it could be, and this is what Dr Wright in her report as an X-ray specialist said, fluid in the lungs from a bit of heart failure, that's called pulmonary oedema. And of course, after the heart has been severely compromised, which is what was happening to [Baby N] at the time we had to resuscitate him and take over his breathing and press on his chest to stimulate his heart, it's possible after that there may be a degree of heart failure causing fluid in the lungs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All of those are possibilities: pulmonary oedema due to heart failure or blood in the lungs or infection in the lungs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The heart failure you refer to was the collapse at 19.40?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So in conclusion, were you able to determine a cause of that collapse?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No. But my best guess at that time in the evening was bleeding into [Baby N]'s lungs. It might have been swelling of the top of his airway, but you'd have to ask Dr Potter whether he saw any swelling when he intubated.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: There was definitely swelling recorded by various colleagues earlier in the afternoon. Dr Potter didn't seem to have a problem but he's very experienced at intubating, at getting the tube in.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the collapse might have been due to swelling of the airway blocking off if Dr Potter feels the airway was still swollen and blocked when he put the tube in.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: As I said, we have to cover for infection without knowing the result of the tests we do to look for infection. In the end, over the next few days on the intensive care unit at Alder Hey Hospital, all the tests for infection proved negative. The blood tests that had been taken from [Baby N] on the morning of 15th by [Dr A], that proved negative. The white cell count and the CRP protein never rose in [Baby N]. So it looks unlikely that his deterioration on 15 June was due to infection. But at the time we were dealing with him, we did not know that and we were covering him for possible infection. But in the end, I don't think infection was the cause of his deterioration.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you remain there and answer any further questions?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Gibbs, at the time you came on duty who was managing the situation with [Baby N]?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Do you mean which consultant was managing it?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes, who would be responsible for that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Dr Saladi was responsible at the time I came on and then I took over from him.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So you came on at about 18.00 hours, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: About then, yes, or slightly before.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Dr Saladi was managing it at that point?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And then it was your responsibility to manage the situation after he had finished; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So you were managing or had responsibility for managing the situation when we get into the period around about 7.20 pm?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Just so that we can be quite clear what your involvement was just leading up to that, we've looked at the records with you contacting the ENT team at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So we can follow this through, was that because you were making preparation in the event that it was necessary to perform an emergency tracheostomy on [Baby N]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. But before that might have become necessary, that would have meant [Baby N]'s airway had failed, the laryngeal mask airway, and it would be my intention for myself to have attempted intubation, but I was aware that various colleagues had failed earlier in the day.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And if that intubation had failed and his airway was blocked off, he might need a tracheostomy, but we might be able to support him with another laryngeal mask or by bag-mask ventilation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The tracheostomy would be, in the circumstances, the last thing you would want to do?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but you have to do it if the airway is blocked off and you can't secure the airway.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Would that be a unusual step to take for a neonate at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So is that why you were taking steps to prepare a theatre should it become necessary to do so that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. And the intention was the specialist team from Alder Hey would perform the tracheostomy. But the reason I'd alerted our local ENT team is just in case that became necessary before the team from Alder Hey arrived, but they did arrive shortly afterwards, fortunately.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: When [Baby N] deteriorated around about 19.40, 7.40 pm, you were close by but not with him; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And I think you have described to us you were in the area outside nursery 1 making arrangements for whatever course might come next?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. I was standing near the entrance way to nursery 1 and I'd been moving in and out of nursery 1, talking to the various colleagues that I have described already, and trying to make sure we had the equipment that they needed. So I might have been just inside nursery 1 or just outside it. But there's an open doorway into nursery 1.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You've been asked various questions about what was the cause of the collapse at 19.40. You've heard those questions being asked by the prosecution.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I want to go back to something that you said early on when you were going through the steps with [Baby N]. You said this about 19.40:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "His oxygen dropped to 80% and his heart rate was down to 60% then down to 40% on the oxygen."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In fact, if it helps I'll put the note up so we're not trying to remember it. Could we put up tile 292, please, Mr Murphy?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This is just so you can keep track of what you said and we can as well, Dr Gibbs. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You have told us the oxygen dropped to 80%. That's in your evidence to us. Then the heart rate goes down to 60. Is that where we can see, about five lines down, it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "... leading to bradycardia of 60 per min"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then oxygen levels dropped down to 40% next, didn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right. In my third line down, I say:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Sudden deterioration, 19.40, as described overleaf by [Dr D]."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Because [Dr D] was the registrar, she had about an hour before me, 21.05, recorded a more detailed account of the resuscitation. Rather than repeat everything she'd put down -and she was assisting during the resuscitation -- I'm referring back to her notes as well. So if it's helpful, if there's any particular point, we might have to look back at her notes as well.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We've got them, just to reassure you, and we've seen them and we can go back to them if we need to. It's this. You then said this about the desaturation and the heart rate dropping:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "It's clear he wasn't being ventilated properly at that time with the LMA in situ."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Which is the laryngeal mask?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You touched on it earlier. Can you explain to us, so we can follow, what's the link between potential problems with his saturation and the LMA, if there is one?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, the laryngeal mask airway is the conduit, the apparatus, through which oxygen and air is being delivered from the ventilator down into [Baby N]'s airway.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Now, if the laryngeal mask has slipped, moved or even folded over on itself, the little oval mask at the bottom of the tube that's sitting above the voice box, if that folds over on itself or the tube is moved, then that can block air and oxygen getting down into the airway.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But also, if there was a swelling of the airway just underneath, below the laryngeal mask, if that swelling has worsened -- and several colleagues saw swelling of the airway when they looked down in the afternoon -- that swelling could stop any ventilation of his lungs because that swelling of his own tissues at the top of his airway could block his airway off and the laryngeal mask would be useless above a completely blocked airway.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If he had been dexamethasone and it had had the effect you said, we know he was given at 17.35, in fact that swelling shouldn't have been a problem in that way if it was no longer preventing intubation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's uncertain how much the dexamethasone will reduce swelling of the airway. It's intended to reduce it. So without looking down -- and Dr Potter is the only one who looked down while I was on the unit -- without looking down, I wouldn't know
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: if the swelling had reduced or gone away completely. But, yes, the swelling should have been less of a problem after the dexamethasone.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But as it happens, as we get to 19.40, there were problems in getting oxygen into [Baby N] in the way that would have been desirable?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So one factor that may play a part in the desaturation that took place was that the oxygen he was receiving through the LMA may not have been as effective as would have been desirable?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And is that why that is one of the issues you have issued which plays a part, whatever part that is --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- in what took place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You also identify the question of the extent to which any swelling that was present myself interfered, for instance, with the fit of the mask?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, or even without the fit of the mask, if -- the swelling would be below the mask, therefore it doesn't -- the laryngeal mask airway would be inadequate, in fact could be completely unhelpful at ventilating [Baby N] if the swelling had blocked his airway off.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: An endotracheal tube passing past the swelling, down into the windpipe, wouldn't have got blocked off by the swelling.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So as to why at that point there is a desaturation, a significant feature potentially is the fact that he was being ventilated by an LMA and we might have just reached the point at which it was failing to do all that was required?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. But in order to have failed, there either had to be swelling blocking off below the laryngeal mask airway or it had moved in some way. The other possibility was that he could have bled. Blood in his oropharynx had been noticed by several people that looked down earlier in the day. If he'd bled again then the blood could have filled his windpipe and might have stopped him being ventilated.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: There wasn't any blood that I could see around at the time, but again Dr Potter is the only person who looked down at his windpipe.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We'll hear from Dr Potter shortly and, this isn't meant to sound rude, but we'll stick to exactly what he could say he saw rather than possibilities with blood.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As to the mask, the LMA, looking at the note you have made four lines down, you've got:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Very difficult to ventilate via LMA (Dr Lakin)."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Had Dr Lakin been using the LMA around the point of the desaturation or do you simply not know?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, initially Dr Lakin tried to ventilate [Baby N] through the laryngeal mask airway and couldn't do so. So he took the laryngeal mask airway out and continued to ventilate him with a bag and mask, so a mask directly over [Baby N]'s mouth and nose.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that the Alder Hey team had arrived, hadn't they, some time shortly before the deterioration [Baby N] suffered?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, and Dr Lakin was one of the team members who had taken over his ventilation when he deteriorated, when he collapsed.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right. Thank you, Dr Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: My Lord, I have no re-examination. Does the court have any questions for Dr Gibbs?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Gibbs, for coming back and giving evidence again. Will he be required again?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So what I've said to you before applies: don't talk to anyone about the case.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
My Lord, I hand over to Mr Astbury to call the next witness.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
If you could state your full name for the record, please.

blocks.text: Thank you. You given evidence before. If you can make sure you keep your voice up, please. Even though I'm the one asking the questions, we'd be very grateful.

blocks.text: You have come along this afternoon to assist with your treatment of a baby by the name of [Baby N].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Which took place on the afternoon of 15 June 2016?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: In preparing a statement in that regard, you have summarised [Baby N]'s history up until that date, day 13 of his life. blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And you have reminded yourself of those in preparing the statement; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You were aware, I think, that blood was noted in the oropharynx during the course of the morning; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. And you, I think, were on duty that afternoon in the Countess of Chester.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was at work, but I was called by my colleague, Dr Saladi, who was the on-call consultant.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Do you recall what time you were called?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Some time in the afternoon.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Okay. Do you remember why you were called?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because Dr Saladi and his team were having difficulty intubating [Baby N].
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Were you made aware that [Baby N] had suffered a further desaturation that afternoon?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, I went to the neonatal unit and Dr Saladi gave me a summary of the events up until that point and then I attempted to intubate [Baby N] as well.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. It's not your note, but so it assists you, could we have, please, tile 246, Mr Murphy?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can see a note there. Again, not your handwriting, Dr Brearey?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: But we can see that you are certainly mentioned, I think. About halfway down it says:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Laryngeal airway placed by Dr Brearey."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I don't know whether you just want to have a look at the note and remind yourself of perhaps what you were told and what the situation was that you came upon.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't quite see who wrote the note. It looks like Dr Saladi's handwriting.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So I would have checked his record afterwards. But Dr Saladi mentioned that [Baby N] had desaturated that afternoon at 2.50 pm and had bled in the oropharynx and...

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And blood in the NG tube, yes:
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: "Improved with bagging [which is Neopuffing [Baby N]]. Electively intubated following [sorry] pre-medication. Unsuccessful attempts with two registrars and two consultants."
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So I believe that would have been [Dr D], Dr Mayberry as the two registrars, and Dr Saladi and myself recorded on that:
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: "Cords difficult to visualise."
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I'd concur with that from memory. And:
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: "Laryngeal airway placed by Dr Brearey and myself."
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm not sure whether a laryngeal airway has been explained to the jury yet.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Before we do that, could we rewind a little bit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you for helping with the note. You've included yourself as one of the two consultants who unsuccessfully attempted to intubate. We're familiar with intubation. Could you just tell us your recollection, please, of your attempts to intubate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't have too much recollection of the reason for not being able to intubate that afternoon. But certainly from a number of records that I've reviewed of the notes since then, it would appear that there was blood in the oropharynx and there was swelling around and above the vocal cords that was making the view difficult.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: All right. So we've heard quite a bit this morning about what has to be visualised, what can and can't.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We're told that the vocal cords ideally have to be visualised because that is where the tube will pass; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: That indicates where the trachea is?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Could you recall what difficulties you were having in visualising that particular part of [Baby N]'s anatomy?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From memory it seemed to be that there was a combination of the larynx being anterior -- feeling more anterior than perhaps we would expect to see.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: What does that mean, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That means when you're having a look with the laryngoscope blade, you can't see the whole of the cords, you can only see the lower section of the vocal cords. blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Are you able to recall, please say if you can't, whereabouts the swelling was precisely?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't precisely recall that myself.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: When you talk about the larynx being anterior, is there a cause for that or is that just an anatomical feature?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it's just a variation in different babies.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I don't think there's any certainty about that at the time, no.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: There's mention in the note of blood. Do you recall seeing any blood?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't, no.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So certainly you would agree that you struggled to intubate in the way that would ordinarily be the case?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Do you happen to remember in what order you came out of those four medical professionals?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was fourth.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Okay. You were going to tell us what the alternative was that you eventually chose.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we have a difficult airway trolley because we sometimes have to deal with a difficult airway, particularly with much smaller babies. One of the options there, which I thought was most appropriate, was to use a laryngeal mask. The brand is called an I-Gel.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: It represents -- if you like, rather than the ET tube on its own, at the end of the tube it's a small mask that fits over the vocal cords area of the airway to provide as much of a seal as possible without actually passing a tube through the cords.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So is it a tube in itself?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's a tube in itself, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: It fits inside, presumably, the oral cavity?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: How far does it extend into the baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It extends all the way to the point of the epiglottis and the vocal cords and then it's designed in a way -- it looks like a small mask, if you like, that actually fits over the vocal cords themselves.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So rather than making a seal at the front of the mouth is it making the seal --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The seal with an ET tube would be at the point of the vocal cords because those vocal cords would sit on the ET tube. But you're not passing the tube through the vocal cords, you're just sitting something on the top of it, making, you know, a loose fit over the top of the vocal cords.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So the seal in fact is further forward than it would be in the event of successful intubation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's closer to the mouth, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY
