blocks.text: I've told you the respiratory status of the baby was relatively stable and the baby improved, [Baby N] improved dramatically 3 days after being in intensive care at Alder Hey. There were no anatomical abnormalities identified by the ENT team or the cardiac team, who looked at the heart and the blood vessels.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: We know there was no evidence of an infection and although blood was seen in the oropharynx, it must have been a small amount of blood because the haemoglobin levels were normal in this baby. So I can think of no natural, normal cause for why [Baby N] deteriorated multiple times as he did and then improved so dramatically afterwards.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: By afterwards, you mean once he'd been transferred?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Exactly, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Does my Lord have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Questions from THE JUDGE
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: At the very beginning you said there wasn't any evidence of pulmonary haemorrhage on the X-ray.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Could pulmonary haemorrhage be excluded then completely?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Not entirely excluded on X-ray. But it was reported by a paediatric haematologist who is used to reporting on newborn babies' X-rays and there was no evidence in the report -- on either report of the two X-rays [Baby N] had of any evidence. I mean, I did a literature search prior to coming to court, looking for reports of pulmonary haemorrhage in preterm babies or newborn babies with haemophilia and I could only find one report in 2021 claiming to be the first report of a baby with haemophilia who had pulmonary haemorrhage, but that baby was 29 weeks, it was born 10 weeks -- sorry, 5 weeks earlier in gestation, much smaller than [Baby N] was, and much smaller and had been on a ventilator for a week prior to that pulmonary haemorrhage.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So you know, this is exceedingly rare and for [Baby N] to be in air, not needing any respiratory support --
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: No need to repeat yourself.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It just doesn't -- it's so, so very rare.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: It was just at the very beginning of that answer you said that and I just wanted to be clear as to the extent it could be excluded or not. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Again?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, we think we'll see Dr Brearey again.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you very much for coming and giving evidence. You will be coming back, so please don't talk to anyone about this case in the meantime.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
My Lord, Dr Francis Potter.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR FRANCIS POTTER (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Could we begin with your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I am Francis Anthony Potter.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Thank you. And your occupation, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm a consultant paediatric anaesthetist.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you become a consultant paediatric anaesthetist back in 1996?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I did, yes, 1 April.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll put that date aside for a moment! Was that at Alder Hey?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: And have you worked there ever since?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Do you have a particular interest in your practice?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: My particular thing is paediatric intensive care --
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Thank you. Do you have particular experience with airway difficulties?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I do. Of the group of consultants on the intensive care unit, I have the most experience of airway problems.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Are you talking about Alder Hey amongst that group?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: How many paediatricians are we talking about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it's 10 or 11 full-time equivalent.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: You've been asked along today to assist us with your treatment of a baby by the name of [Baby N] --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: -- as long ago as 15 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Now, do you have any independent recollection of [Baby N]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I remembered the case quite -- well, bits of the case very well because it was quite unusual. Normally, children from other hospitals who need intensive care at Alder Hey, the usual process is for the hospital who have got the problem patient to contact what's called NWTS, that's the North-west Paediatric Transfer Service.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And they ring us to check that we've got a bed, but NWTS actually send out an ambulance and a team of either a registrar or consultant from NWTS to the hospital and bring --
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: We've heard a little bit about that system. Are you leading up to say this was a little bit different?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This was a bit unusual. I can't remember now whether we got the call directly from NWTS or whether it was from Chester. But they said that the problem was that they had this child who was ill and needed to come to Alder Hey for intensive care, but they couldn't intubate him.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Right. I'm going to ask you to pause there. Have you checked the notes during the course of the preparation of your statement?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Would it assist to see some notes as we go along?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: I'm going to ask Mr Murphy, who's behind me, to put up tile 291, please, just with regard to who contacted you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we go behind it, please, and scroll down.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So certainly by 6 o'clock, I think that's a phone call from you; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From what that said, yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: I think if we go down a little bit, I'm not sure whether it's this page, you'd certainly been contacted by 6 o'clock?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: We can see some of the arrangements that were being made if that assists you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Basically, this call had come through to the ICU at Alder Hey and they'd explained the situation, that they had been -- they'd attempted to intubate this baby and hadn't been able to do so. And I knew some of the people involved in that.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: At Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At Chester. That was [Dr C], who was one of the consultant paediatricians there, and Dr Brearey. They'd both worked at Alder Hey for about 6 months on the intensive care unit, so I knew them reasonably well.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: When I heard that they had had trouble intubating this child, I realised that -- I surmised that this would be a genuinely difficult case.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I thought then that the best way of dealing with this would be for me to go out to Chester to intubate the child.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Is that what you did?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Again, I was anticipating that this would be very difficult, so I have taken some -- I drove out to Chester, taking some specialist equipment with me. That was a very small, flexible telescope that you can use for intubating someone who is difficult to intubate. So rather than using a conventional laryngoscope, I was taking out a special bit of kit to do so.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Was that a flexible bronchoscope?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. You can call it different things, but a flexible --
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: I'm just looking at the note, that's all.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, that would be a flexible bronchoscope.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you. So you made the decision to set off from Chester, you selected some kit to take with you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: You were given, were you, before you left, a summary of the issues that were the problem? I think you were told that [Baby N] was suffering with apnoeas; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Did that strike you in itself as problematic?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: That the team at Chester had been unable to intubate his windpipe. There was a concern of a pulmonary haemorrhage. Were you told that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I remember that, yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: And that he was having his airway supported but was breathing for himself?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: So we've just looked at the note a moment or two ago.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A [Dr D] noted that you arrived at Chester at 19.15 hours. Does that accord with your recollection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um... I can't recall at this distance exactly what time it was.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Do you recall having anyone with you when you went to Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Again, I can't quite recall. Another of my consultant colleagues on the paediatric intensive care unit, Dr Ben Lakin — and I can't quite recall if he came in the car with me -- and possibly an ENT surgeon from Alder Hey came with us as well. But I really -- I know that Dr Lakin was at Chester during the actual time we were there. I can't quite recall how he got there.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Okay. That may not be important. Don't worry about that.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we can go next, please, to tile 316. These tile numbers are just to assist with our presentation, Dr Potter, if you'll bear with me when I'm shouting these numbers out.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think this is a nursing note which suggests that you arrived between 7.00 and 7.15. Do you recall what you did when you first arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I got the special intubating bronchoscope out of my car and went into the paediatric block at Chester and I started -- I may have briefly -- I can't recall absolutely. I may have briefly seen the patient but I do remember that we started to get the stuff ready for doing a fibre-optic intubation, so I was assembling the kit.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: I think you told us about the -- I'm not going to attempt to say it -- the flexible tube that you can use?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Which is a little more sophisticated than the laryngoscope that we've heard about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Normally, you use a laryngoscope, which is a sort of C-shaped bit of metal that you insert into the mouth to light up the view of the voice box, the larynx.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: We've heard a little bit about that. What was the advantage of your bit of kit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, with the kit that I have, a fibre-optic scope, it's very flexible and you put the scope down the tube that you want to pass into the windpipe through the voice box and then you can look through the scope and either pass that, usually through the nose, through the nose, through the back of the mouth, view the larynx, view the voice box, pass the scope into the windpipe and then you pass the tube -- the tube is mounted on the scope -- and you then just wriggle the tube in over the scope into the windpipe.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: So it's guided through?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Did you get that far? Did you get to look at the voice box using that equipment?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. As I was -- I was still assembling the fibre-optic scope, because that needs its own light source and that all needs to be assembled. As I was doing that, the sort of -- the arrest bleep went off for this baby.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Can you recall where you were at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was in a room immediately near the baby.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: So within the vicinity (overspeaking).
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think I must have been within the unit, yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: But not in the same room?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not when the arrest bleep went off.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: When I say the arrest bleep, I mean someone -- I don't know whether -- exactly if there was a bleep or whether someone physically came into the room and said the child's arrested.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Was anyone with you while you were doing that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There would have been -- I think Dr Lakin was probably with me by then. Anyway, when I heard that, I left the scope and went in to where the child was.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: What did you find? What did you initially find?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The baby had a -- was mottled and greyish.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Did you make a note of this at the time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not directly at the time, but shortly afterwards I've noted what I'd seen.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Perhaps, rather than ask you to remember every detail, would it help to see your note?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Could we have page J19382, please, Mr Murphy. We'll enlarge it. Do you recognise the handwriting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Afraid so.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Okay. Is that:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Called to see infant while preparing theatre for intubation"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I was preparing theatre for intubation.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Just take us through your note, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. So:
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: "Infant very pale and mottled. Bradycardic."
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: That means a slow heart rate, of 60 beats a minute.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: That probably sounds normal to a layperson, but in a newborn baby that heart rate really isn't sufficient to have a circulation working properly.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Okay. We've heard that's a point at which intervention follows?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely. And in particular, because this baby also has an arterial oxygen saturation measured by that SPO2, it's less than 40, so it's no longer accurate down at those sort of levels, a pulse oximeter, but it suggests the child was very, very short of oxygen. And by the time your heart has slowed from being short of oxygen, you are at the point of arrest, so something needs to be done immediately in that circumstance.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Okay. So what follows?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think from that, it says the child was still making some respiratory effort and it had an LMA, which means a laryngeal mask airway. That was in the child's mouth, acting as an airway. So that laryngeal mask sort of points towards the voice box, but doesn't pass through the voice box.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: We've heard a little bit about that. So what (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I took that out and held a face mask over the child and then artificially -- tried to artificially ventilate the child using what's called a bag and mask circuit.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Okay. Do you remember anyone who was with you at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: All right. So bag and mask. Did that have a positive effect?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It didn't really. I think I noted there, the SPO2 was not really improving.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: That's the oxygen saturation which is below 40?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So at that point we started doing ECCM, that means we did external closed chest cardiac massage, so we then started --
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: CPR --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: CPR.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: -- as we call it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: On this baby, yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Carry on with your note, if you don't mind.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the child is given some adrenaline. I presume the child -- from that, the child must have had some IV access.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But through a peripheral line because normally you'd use 1:10,000 adrenaline in an arrest situation but we're using a slightly more dilute form of adrenaline, 1:20,000, which is giving a bigger volume.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: We can see, "Right foot peripheral line"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. The pulse then speeded up but the SpO2 remained low. So the pulse increasing in speed is what you'd expect having given the child adrenaline, but really, the child is still very hypoxic because we haven't got a good airway at this stage.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Then is that "direct" --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I then used an ordinary laryngoscope to look into this child's mouth and I could see the back half of the voice box.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Okay. Describe to us what you saw. Was there anything unusual about what you saw?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um... No. There was no... What I feared was seeing a lot of blood and sort of a distorted picture because I knew that this child had had multiple attempts at getting this tube in, in the way that I was doing it.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And I think by that time, I also knew that there'd been talk of the pulmonary haemorrhage and I'm pretty sure that even by this time I knew that the child's mum was a haemophilia carrier so there was a 50% chance that this child would have haemophilia.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So if there had been any trauma to the voice box or any of the structures inside the mouth, there was a reasonable chance of blood being there. I can recall that -- I couldn't recall, if -- that's like a double negative... I recall at the
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: time thinking, well, there's no blood here. I could see the arytenoid cartilages which mark the furthest back part of the voice box and so I was able to pass a bougie, which is a sort of very, very thin plastic stick, flexible stick, between the arytenoid cartilages, through the hole, as it were, in the voice box.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: And that's the --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Having got that bougie in, I was then able to pass a tube over the bougie into the windpipe.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Is that a similar principle to -- you were telling us about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: The tube goes over the guide --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: -- and you're able to slide it over the top?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Okay. So you were able to visualise the relevant point, if I put it that way --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: -- in the voice box behind the two structures that you told us?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So the voice box has these -- the voice box (inaudible) hole like that (indicating). And what I was looking at were these two structures here, the arytenoid cartilages. So I knew the -- you know that you've put a tube into the -through the voice box and into the trachea, into the windpipe if you can see the tube passing in front of those cartilages and not behind those cartilages. Behind those cartilages you're passing a tube into the gullet, into the food pipe, and you can't ventilate the lungs if the tube is in the food pipe.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: But I could see that first the bougie and then the tube over it had passed anterior to those cartilages and were lying then in the windpipe. And that was confirmed then because you get -carbon dioxide only comes out of the windpipe, not out of the food pipe, and they had a little device that changes colour when it's exposed to carbon dioxide.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Is that a capnograph?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We were able to put that on the tube and with this carbon dioxide that came out of the lungs, that changed colour, so we knew that the tube was in the windpipe.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: So I think the rest of your note talks about the bougie inserted and three --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A size 3-millimetre tube.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Is that "railroaded"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Was railroaded, yes, over, over the bougie.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: All right. And then is that "hand ventilation"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Hand ventilation in 100% oxygen, good chest movement, positive CO2 colour change, but only slow improvement of the saturation beyond the 60s."
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: So you'd expect, if the child was entirely well and we've intubated it and you're ventilating the child in 100% oxygen, you'd expect the saturation on the oximeter to be 90-plus. This one was still in the 60s, so it was going up, but it was still pretty low.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Do it take it from that you'd have expected it to go up quicker?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: If we can scroll down to the rest of your note.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that, "Given sodium bicarbonate"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He was given sodium bicarbonate, a bolus of that, because the child -- the assumption is that the child would be very acidotic having been without oxygen or with a very low oxygen for so long, and it's just immediately sort of post an arrest situation. And we've then given -- an adrenaline infusion was then started via the peripheral line. So having given boluses of adrenaline, we're now giving a continuous infusion of adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: By this time the NWTS team had arrived.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Yes. This is the transport team?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the transport team. So the transport team will have come from Warrington, their base, and I come from Alder Hey, so by this time everyone who was needed was there.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Just before that, we've got tube fixed; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Then just take us through the next part, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that, "IJ line"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So we've got the adrenaline running through a peripheral line. Adrenaline causes the blood vessels to constrict a lot and you really -- a drug like adrenaline should be given via a central line, that's a big venous -- a big vein, essentially, that runs pretty directly into the heart so that you can be absolutely sure that the child is getting the dose of adrenaline that you think you are giving it. So I think I inserted that right internal jugular line (indicating).
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: So that's into -- you're pointing to your neck. That's into the neck?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It's into the jugular vein in the neck. As I say, the NWTS team has arrived and the doctor with the NWTS team, Chris Goodwin, then looked to pass an arterial line into the femoral artery in this child. This is standard intensive care monitoring and a standard way of giving an intensive care infusion of a drug like adrenaline. He actually struggled a little bit to get that arterial line in so I ended up taking over from him in doing that. And then we had the arterial line in so we could measure the child's blood pressure and do arterial gases and make any further alterations into the dose of adrenaline that we had to give to maintain a good circulation and giving the child fluid. And then basically, they were sort of preparing to move the child then from Chester to the intensive care unit at Alder Hey.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: So at that point, presumably the transport team take over?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Would you then have really concluded with your treatment of --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I think I -- yes. Having established that the transport team were quite happy to transport the child to Alder Hey, I then left and went home.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Okay. In preparing your statement, you've told us that you're a consultant at Alder Hey. You've also summarised [Baby N]'s progress after he'd arrived at Arrowe Park; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: After Alder Hey.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It was fairly uneventful, basically. By the time he got to Alder Hey it was just after midnight, so it's then down as the 16th.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He had remained on the adrenaline infusion following this episode of effective cardiac arrest that he'd had at Chester. But my colleagues were able to fairly quickly decrease the amount of adrenaline that the baby was requiring to maintain his circulation overnight. He needed ventilation but in not very much oxygen and not very high pressures over the course of that night and the following day, I think into the following day. But he was able to be fairly rapidly taken off the ventilator. So he's only on the intensive care unit for, I think, about 48 hours, something like that and was able to go from the intensive care unit to the high dependency care unit by the Saturday. So this -- I've been involved with this child on the Wednesday evening and then by the Saturday he's able to leave ITU.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Right. Okay. Your note and your statement is he's breathing for himself by the afternoon of the 18th?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: All right. Did he continue to suffer with episodes of apnoea?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, he did. They were less frequent and altogether less troublesome, but they did require some further investigation.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Apnoea in a child of this age is one of those things that can be simply a sign that the child is unwell for many reasons, really, or you can have specific reason, some specific reason why the child might have apnoea.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: I think that the child ends up being given, I think, some -- on the ward is given a medication to guard against apnoeas and to decrease their frequency. That's caffeine.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That was kept on for a good few days and then stopped and then they just observed the child. But then I think subsequently, the child ended up being readmitted to Alder Hey, but not to the intensive care unit.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But was readmitted for some further investigation of these apnoeas, which he had by means of -- he has, I think, an MR scan of his head, looking at the brain, to see if there was anything specific within the brain that might give rise to apnoeas, and there wasn't. He also had an ENT examination of his voice box and trachea to see if there was anything there that might give rise to problems with apnoea, and again that drew a blank.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Any abnormalities detected on that particular examination?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't think there were, no.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: From what you saw on the evening of the 15th when you successfully intubated [Baby N], are you able to say what may have caused the problems or did you not see anything?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It wasn't an entirely straightforward view of the voice box. You would normally, in a baby of this size, expect to be able to see pretty well all of the voice box quite clearly and I was only able to see the back half of the voice box. It's possible to have completely normal anatomy and still be not entirely -- still have a not entirely normal view of the larynx, the voice box.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Getting a good view of the voice box with an ordinary laryngoscope depends on being able to push the tongue forwards and out of the way.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Now, your tongue in fact isn't just the top bit you see in your mouth, it's sort of got -- it's sort of an inverted L shape, your tongue. You need to be able to move the vertical bit of the tongue forwards and it's attached to your lower jaw. So if your lower jaw is a bit receding, a bit backwards, then there isn't room to push the tongue forwards. And if you can't push the tongue forwards, you can only see the back half of the voice box.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Now, this can be occasionally just the way things are, particularly in a newborn, and then as the child grows in size, the jaw itself may even fractionally just move a little bit
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: further forwards and you can then see the voice box more clearly when you look in with a conventional laryngoscope.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: In fact, I noted that this child, [Baby N], came back for an operation when he was 9 kilos, having been 1.7 kilos at the time I saw him. He was intubated by one of my colleagues and she said that, again, it was straightforward but there needed to be some external pressure on his neck to push his voice box back that little bit more so that she could get an entirely clear view of his voice box.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: So I took it that he was just one of these infants in whom the view is more difficult than usual but they sort of easily grow out of it rather than having any specific anatomical problem with the voice box.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Do you recall when you came to intubate him that evening whether there was any swelling of the epiglottis?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't recall that. Basically, in this sort of situation, what you're looking for is the hole and you want to get the tube in the hole. What's surrounding it, you're less interested in.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: I have no more questions. If you could wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Just to reassure everybody, I'll be about 15 minutes, my Lord, Dr Potter. This is the slot I have.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It was apparent to you, wasn't it, when you got to the unit that a number of practitioners had attempted to intubate [Baby N] and they just hadn't been able to do so?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: You'd been informed that there'd been an issue with that before you went, hadn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I knew that they'd had trouble intubating this child before I set off from Alder Hey; that's why I took the specialist equipment.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: The bronchoscope and things like that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: All right. Just getting right down to the question of the intubation, when it came to you dealing with it, you really didn't encounter great difficulty, did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It wasn't the most straightforward I've ever done, it was more difficult than usual, but, no, I didn't have great difficulty in doing it.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: You didn't need to use a bronchoscope as it happens, did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: So you were able to do this using a laryngoscope, which is the piece of equipment the doctors at the unit had used?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: You were able to use, was it a 3-millimetre -- a 3.0 tube?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. A 3-millimetre internal diameter tube to intubate the child's voice box.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Which in your view, I'm looking at your statement here, is pretty unremarkable for an infant of his size?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, for a 1.7-kilogram infant you'd expect to get a 3.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Nothing from your experience that got in the way of you being able to intubate as it happens?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: And as we've seen your note, certainly no reference to any swelling at the time that you dealt with it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: And no reference to any blood?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: So let me put it this way: for you, it was something you managed to do with relative ease. I'm not suggesting it was easy, but with relative ease?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: And nothing like as complicated as you'd expected from what you'd been told beforehand?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: That's for you. On the other hand, was it your assessment when you look at all of this that for doctors who don't have the experience that you have, it may have presented some challenges?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: All right. And a doctor without your experience, or with less experience, might find this difficult if not impossible to do; was that your view?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: You have just explained to us a feature of [Baby N]'s anatomy as best as you can recall that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Which was that it was more difficult, was it, to get a view at a certain part of his voice box looking down into the trachea?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, to see the voice -- to get a tube into his windpipe, you have to see -- the opening is the voice box. The opening to the windpipe is within the voice box. So you have to get a good view of the voice box to get a tube in the windpipe. To get a good view of the voice box, it's necessary to move both the tongue and the epiglottis out of your line of sight. And I think in [Baby N]'s case, it was more difficult to do that than usual in a baby.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: And that's something that can follow simply from the way that his tongue and the soft tissues around that part of the body were structured at that time in his life?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Notwithstanding that, would you expect that, for instance, consultants in a neonatal unit would be able to deal with this?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um... Yes. Most of the time, yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: All right. One of the matters you described, which informs your view of [Baby N], was that there was an operation he had when he was 11 months old, wasn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: You made reference to that. Was it Dr Rodrigues, your colleague, who said it wasn't entirely straightforward dealing with the intubation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, she'd just made a little note on the anaesthetic sheet that she wrote at that time, saying he needed cricoid pressure, that is external pressure on the neck, to press the voice box back a little bit to make it easier to get the tube in.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: So that's called cricoid pressure?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: And that's just down on the lower part of the trachea, is it --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The upper part (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: -- near to the Adam's apple?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She needed to do that to make it work with [Baby N] when she did the intubation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. But that's... That might be the case in 5%, 10% of cases that we do.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Did you need to use cricoid pressure at all yourself when you dealt with [Baby N] initially or can you not recall?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't recall. I probably did, but I can't quite recall.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: It's something you would understand might be necessary in dealing with a child in that situation if it's a little difficult to visualise?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: And that comes from your experience, the level at which you work?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Just something slightly different, Dr Potter. If a baby, a neonate, undergoes a series of intubations or attempted intubations, can that series of intubations in itself add to the physical stress upon the baby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry? I don't quite... I don't understand what you mean by physical stress.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: The easiest thing is can I ask you to look at page 3311 of your statement. I'm going to ask Mr Murphy to put up page 3311 so you have it in front of you. It's a statement you made on 9 April 2019.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: It's the fourth page and it's just the paragraph that starts:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "It is important to consider the circumstances..."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: I'm just going to ask you to read that paragraph to yourself and then I'll just go over with it you, please.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: That was quick. Have you read it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I'm very familiar with it.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Okay. You make the observation that:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "An initial failure [this is to do with intubation] is likely to have produced a fall in the baby's saturation..."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: "... (which may have been lower than normal here to begin with), which almost invariably adds stress to the next attempt.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And even putting stress apart, it's now well recognised that views at difficult laryngoscopy tend to deteriorate with repeated attempts."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. So what I meant by that was, it's stress on the part of the person trying to intubate.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Sorry, I misunderstood that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If you're trying to get this tube in to maintain the life of an infant and you go to a -- and you expect to be able to do this straightforwardly, and you look in and it's not straightforward, and you do what you think should produce the desired results, the tube passing into the windpipe, and it fails, so you then sort of re-group and try and do it again and in the meantime you can hear the saturation falling from the note on the oximeter and you're looking again and you may not be able to see any of the structures that you want to see in order
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: to get this tube in and you're aware that the baby's oxygen levels are falling and you're trying to stay calm and simply intubate the windpipe again.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: If you're failing to do that then everything becomes more difficult and you're aware that the oxygen saturations are falling and that the child's in front of you and the child's going a little bit blue and its heart rate is falling and you're aware that if things go on like this for much longer, the child is going to have a cardiac arrest. So you have to stay calm in that situation or try to.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: It is known now that -- it's been demonstrated in a number of studies that your best chance of intubating an infant is your first attempt, as it were, and failure makes the second attempt more difficult and the third more difficult and it just becomes a law of diminishing returns. There has been in general throughout the whole of anaesthesia an idea that rather than making repeated attempts at intubation, attempts at intubation are limited and you then rapidly move to getting someone with more experience to do the job rather than repeatedly trying.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Thank you for explaining that. In this case, of course, we know that, because you explained how for an individual practitioner it may become difficult with repeated attempts.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Of course one feature of this case is there was a whole series of practitioners who all had attempts to intubate [Baby N], weren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That's why I was anticipating that this would be very difficult because I knew at least some of the people involved and I thought they were pretty competent.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: What was the word, sorry?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Pretty competent and would be able to, you know...
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: You would expect it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Finally this, Dr Potter: you were asked some questions just about [Baby N] after the key date that we've just been looking at.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: [Baby N] was judged safe to go home on 26 June 2016.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that was a typo --
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- on my part, I think.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: He was readmitted to Alder Hey, having been at home on 3 July 2016, wasn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: There had been further episodes of apnoeas and abnormal movements when he was readmitted, hadn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: And he was given breathing support with CPAP and then a number of investigations were undertaken to look for causes for those apnoeas, weren't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: But there was nothing conclusive by way of a definite cause that could explain those; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's how I would interpret the note.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: And in any event, in due course, that settled and there was no continuing problem so far as you're aware?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's the case.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Potter.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I have nothing arising. Does my Lord have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Questions from THE JUDGE
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just one question, and you may or may not be able to answer this: would the administration of adrenaline and/or steroids have any effect on swelling?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Um... Possibly. Do you mean the fact that the child had been on adrenaline, which would reduce swelling to an appreciable degree between... Certainly not between the previous efforts at intubation and mine.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There would not have been time for that --
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: To have had any effect?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Any effect, I don't think.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Steroids?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Again, this had been done. The effects would be fairly marginal in that sort of time course between the last effort on the part of the anaesthetists at Chester and my attempt. I don't think that steroids would have had time to have made a substantial difference to any swelling.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: My Lord, there is another medication that was administered, dexamethasone.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's a steroid. But I would be very surprised if that had sufficient time to --
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Do you know when it was administered and how many times?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Right. I'm not sure what time I intubated.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: You arrived at 19.15. I'm not sure what time you actually...
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. So you wouldn't really expect -- no it, wouldn't make... It certainly wouldn't make a difference such that you'd say, that was very badly swollen and now it isn't. I don't think there would be that --
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: No, I left it as an open, neutral question: any effect on swelling?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Steroids such as dexamethasone do reduce swelling, but usually the time course for that effect is hours into a day or two rather than minutes.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Well, it's not minutes. Here it's 2 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Even after a couple of hours, I would be very, very surprised if that had that sort of effect.
blocks.speaker: POTTER

blocks.text: Right. Thank you. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That completes your evidence, Dr Potter, thank you very much. You won't be required again, so thank you for coming and helping us this afternoon.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
Right. That's it for today then.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, members of the jury. 10.30 tomorrow morning.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Please remember your obligations: no research, no communication.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
Do you want to go down, Mr Myers?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: If we could briefly do so, we'd be grateful, if it's possible.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS
